source_text: Diu sanctitati tuae, coepiscope uenerande Pauline, rescriptorum debitor fui, ex quo mihi scripsisti per homines filiae nostrae religiosissimae Florae, quaerens a me, utrum prosit cuique post mortem, quod corpus eius apud sancti alicuius memoriam sepelitur. hoc enim abs te uidua memorata petiuerat pro defuncto in eis partibus suo filio et rescripseras consolans eam: idque etiam nuntians de cadauere fidelis iuuenis Cynegii, quod materno et pio affectu desiderauit, esse conpletum, ut scilicet in beatissimi Felicis confessoris basilica poneretur. qua occasione factum est, ut per eosdem perlatores litterarum tuarum etiam mihi scriberes, ingerens huiusce modi quaestionem, atque ut responderem quid inde mihi uideretur, exposcens nec tacens ipse quid sentias. nam dicis uideri tibi non esse inanes motus animorum religiosorum atque fidelium pro suis ista curantium. adiungis etiam uacare non posse, quod uniuersa pro defunctis ecclesia supplicare consueuit, ut hinc et illud conici possit, homini prodesse post mortem, si fide suorum humando eius corpori talis prouideatur locus, in quo appareat opitulatio etiam isto modo quaesita sanctorum.
thought_title: Why burial at a holy memorial may help the dead
orientation: Augustine opens his letter to Bishop Paulinus of Nola, answering a question from the widow Flora about whether burial at a saint's memorial shrine benefits the dead.
pass_a_gloss: For a long time I have been a debtor of a reply to your holiness, venerable fellow bishop Paulinus, from the time when you wrote to me through the men of our most religious daughter Flora, asking from me whether it benefits anyone after death that his body is buried at the memorial shrine of some saint. For the remembered widow had asked this of you on behalf of her son deceased in those parts, and you had written back consoling her; and also announcing this about the body of the faithful young man Cynegius, which she desired with maternal and pious affection, that it had been fulfilled, namely that it should be placed in the basilica of the most blessed confessor Felix. By which occasion it happened that through the same bearers of your letters you also wrote to me, pressing a question of this kind, and demanding that I answer what seems to me about it, and not keeping silent yourself about what you think. For you say that it seems to you that the movements of religious and faithful minds caring for these things for their own are not empty. You add also that it cannot be without effect that the whole church has been accustomed to pray for the dead, so that from this also that may be inferred, that it benefits a person after death, if by the faith of his own a place of such kind is provided for burying his body, in which the help of the saints sought also in this way may appear.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'memorial shrine' for memoria, avoiding 'memorial' or 'memory' alone.
The glossary requires 'affection' for affectus, avoiding 'emotion'.
The glossary requires 'prayer' for supplicatio; the verb is rendered 'to pray' to match, avoiding 'supplicate'.
'Body' is the natural English for a corpse in this context, and the passage contrasts body and soul.
Rendered literally to preserve the philosophical sense of inner motions or impulses, not 'emotions'.
The idiom uacare means 'to be empty, idle, without effect'; rendered to keep the negative force.

pass_b_english: I have long owed your Holiness a written reply, venerable fellow bishop Paulinus, ever since you wrote to me through members of the household of our daughter Flora, a most religious woman. You asked me whether it benefits anyone after death if his body is buried at the memorial shrine of some saint. The widow I mentioned had asked you this on behalf of her son, who died in your region, and you had written back to console her. You also told her that her wish concerning the body of the faithful young man Cynegius had been fulfilled—the wish she held with a mother's pious affection—namely, that he should be placed in the basilica of the most blessed confessor Felix. On that occasion it happened that, through the same bearers of your letter, you also wrote to me, raising this kind of question and asking me to answer what I thought about it, while not hiding your own view. For you say it seems to you that the movements of religious and faithful minds caring for their own are not empty. You add also that it cannot be without effect that the whole church is accustomed to pray for the dead, so that from this one may also infer that it helps a person after death if, through the faith of his own people, a place is provided for burying his body where the help of the saints sought in this way may be evident.

last_rejected.quote: members of the household of our daughter Flora
last_rejected.source_quote: per homines filiae nostrae religiosissimae Florae
last_rejected.why: "homines" means men/people, not household members; no word for household.
last_rejected.fix: through men of our most religious daughter Flora
last_rejected.ruling: 'homines' can mean servants/household members; rendering fits context of a religious woman's attendants.

last_rejected.quote: her wish concerning the body of the faithful young man Cynegius
last_rejected.source_quote: de cadauere fidelis iuuenis Cynegii, quod materno et pio affectu desiderauit
last_rejected.why: The antecedent of "quod" is the burial placement, not Flora's wish; Cynegius's mother desired it.
last_rejected.fix: concerning the body of the faithful young man Cynegius, which his mother desired with pious affection
last_rejected.ruling: 'desiderauit' subject is the widow/mother; 'her wish' correctly captures maternal desire for Cynegius's burial.
